title: Monitoring and Controlling Compliance of Abattoir Activities

lessons.title: What to monitor and how
lessons.html:
Monitoring is planned checking

Compliance does not happen by itself. A supervisor must check, at planned times and in a planned way, that activities meet the law and the abattoir's procedures. Monitoring finds problems early, before they become an audit failure, a product recall or an injury.

Areas to monitor

AreaExamples of checks
Animal welfareHandling in the lairage, water available, stunning effectiveness
HygieneHand washing, knife sterilising, carcass contamination, condensation
TemperatureSteriliser water, chillers, carcass deep muscle, dispatch vehicles
CleaningPre-operational checks, cleaning records, chemical strengths
Pest controlBait stations, signs of pests, fly control
Condemned materialMarking, containers, locked storage, removal records
SafetyProtective equipment, machine guards, lock-out, wet floors
RecordsComplete, signed, on time

Methods

  • Observation: walk the section and watch workers at work.
  • Measurement: temperatures, chemical concentrations, carcass counts.
  • Checklists: standard forms so nothing is missed.
  • Record review: check that forms are filled in correctly and on time.
  • Talking to workers: ask them to explain the procedure; this shows if training has worked.
  • Test results: water tests and microbiological swabs from the laboratory.

Vary the time of some checks so they are not always predictable. Practices should be correct all the time, not only when the supervisor is expected.

lessons.title: Taking corrective and preventive action
lessons.html:
When monitoring finds a problem

A non-conformance is any situation where an activity does not meet a requirement. The supervisor must act in two ways:

  • Corrective action deals with the problem now: stop it, fix it, and deal with any product affected.
  • Preventive action stops it happening again by fixing the root cause.

Example

During a check you find the knife steriliser at the evisceration station is below its required temperature.

  1. Immediate correction: stop the worker using that steriliser; provide a working one or a spare knife from another steriliser.
  2. Product: decide with the quality controller or inspector whether carcasses dressed since the last good check need extra attention.
  3. Root cause: was the element faulty? Was the water changed and not given time to heat up? Was the steriliser switched off?
  4. Preventive action: repair, add a check at start-up, train workers.
  5. Record: what, when, who, what was done and the follow-up check.

Finding the root cause: ask why five times

Carcasses are contaminated with gut content. Why? Intestines are being cut. Why? A new worker is doing evisceration. Why? The experienced worker was absent. Why? No one else was trained on that station. Why? There is no multi-skilling plan. Preventive action: train backup workers for critical stations.

Escalation

Some problems are beyond the supervisor. Report to the manager, the meat inspector or the veterinarian when:

  • Unsafe meat may have been passed or dispatched.
  • A notifiable disease is suspected.
  • A serious injury or dangerous incident happened.
  • The same problem keeps returning.

lessons.title: Records, audits and continuous improvement
lessons.html:
If it is not written down, it did not happen

Auditors from the provincial veterinary services and customers judge an abattoir largely on its records. Good records prove compliance and help find trends.

Good record practice

  • Fill in records at the time of the check, never later from memory.
  • Write clearly in pen; cross out mistakes with one line and initial them. Never use correction fluid.
  • Record actual values, such as the temperature measured, not just a tick.
  • Sign and date every entry.
  • File records where they can be found quickly, for the period your procedures require.

Preparing for audits

Treat every day as an audit day. Before a scheduled audit, review records for gaps, check that previous audit findings have been closed, walk the section with a checklist, and brief the team on what to expect. During the audit, answer honestly. Do not hide problems; show what you have done about them.

Using trends

Look at records over weeks and months. Are condemnations for contamination rising? Are chiller temperatures creeping up in summer? Is one station always involved in incidents? Trends show where to put effort and training.

Continuous improvement

Use the plan, do, check, act cycle: plan an improvement, try it, check the results, and make it the standard if it works. Involve workers; they often know the best practical solutions.

Key points

  • Monitor welfare, hygiene, temperature, cleaning, pests, condemned material, safety and records.
  • Use observation, measurement, checklists, record review and talking to workers.
  • Corrective action fixes the problem now; preventive action removes the root cause.
  • Record actual values at the time of the check, and sign them.
  • Use trends and the plan, do, check, act cycle to improve.
